# Wasserstein GAN
The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) is a variant of the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to address critical training issues such as mode collapse, vanishing gradients, and instability inherent in standard GANs. Unlike traditional GANs that rely on Jensen-Shannon divergence, WGAN utilizes the Wasserstein metric (Earth Mover's distance), which provides a more meaningful measure of the distance between the generated data distribution and the real data distribution, even when they do not overlap. To implement this mathematically while ensuring computational efficiency, WGAN constrains the discriminator (or critic) to have a bounded Lipschitz norm. This constraint prevents the discriminator from becoming too powerful too quickly, thereby providing the generator with stable, non-vanishing gradients during training.
To enforce the Lipschitz constraint, WGAN employs several techniques, most notably weight clipping, spectral normalization, and gradient penalty. Weight clipping limits the magnitude of the weights in the critic's neural network, while spectral normalization adjusts the weights based on the spectral radius of the weight matrices to bound the Lipschitz constant dynamically. Alternatively, gradient penalty adds a regularization term to the loss function that penalizes the discriminator if the slope of its output exceeds a specific threshold, ensuring smooth gradients. These modifications allow the generator to learn more effectively and produce higher-quality synthetic data without the common failure modes seen in earlier GAN architectures.
